text: A floral clock, or flower clock, is a large decorative clock where the clock face is formed by carpet bedding and is typically located in a park or public recreation area. Most floral clocks have their mechanism embedded in the ground beneath the flowerbed, which is then planted to visually resemble a clock face with moving hands that may also feature bedding plants. The first floral clock was conceived by John McHattie, Superintendent of Parks in Edinburgh, Scotland, and was first planted in the spring of 1903 in West Princes Street Gardens. It initially included only an hour hand, with a minute hand added the following year. A cuckoo that pops out every quarter hour was added in 1952. The clock was soon replicated across the United Kingdom and later worldwide. In Edinburgh, the clock mechanism is housed within the plinth of the statue to Allan Ramsay. The first mechanism, made from salvaged parts from Elie Parish Church in Fife, was installed by James Ritchie & Son. A new mechanism was installed in 1934 and has been electrically operated since 1973, and it is currently maintained by James Ritchie Clockmakers. The only floral clock with two faces driven by the same system is located in Zacatlán, Puebla, Mexico, and features two faces, each five metres (16 ft) in diameter, built by Relojes Centenario, a local manufacturer. Michael Jackson had a floral clock at his Neverland Ranch. Other examples can be found in the International Peace Garden on the border between North Dakota and Manitoba, Rockford, Illinois, and Frankfort, Kentucky. On 19 May 2016, Camarillo Plaza in California unveiled a 13-foot (4.0 m) diameter floral clock created as a dedication to Mr. David Pick.
